title: Unpleasant meditation-related experiences in regular meditators: Prevalence, predictors, and conceptual considerations

cost.compute_notes: Full text as JATS from Europe PMC (read in full). OSF parent gj7z2 lists zero files -- acquire.py refused it and named the three child components; data (d6mgj: raw 724,604 B + clean 458,064 B xlsx) and script (9zsfb: 2,155 B Stata .do) fetched and hash-verified. Stata script ported to Python; prevalence, Table 1 and every Table 2 odds ratio reproduce to the printed decimals. Four scripts, seconds each. Data not committed (no licence on the OSF node); run_all.sh re-fetches.

claims.statement: 25.6% (95% CI 23.1-28.0) of regular meditators report having had particularly unpleasant experiences they think may have been caused by their meditation practice.
claims.scope: Online convenience survey April-August 2017 via social media, Buddhist communities, meditation centres; English-language; practising at least weekly for >= 2 months; one yes/no item, asked LAST, after the 15-item PTQ, 26-item SCS and 19-item Mindsens.

quantities.name: meditation_unpleasant_experience_lifetime_prevalence
quantities.baseline: current regular meditators (>= weekly, >= 2 months), analytic sample after excluding yoga-only and non-responders

quantities.name: survey_starters_reaching_outcome_item
quantities.baseline: everyone who opened the survey; completion differs by continent (Asia 59%, Europe 72%, Australia 84%) and by religiosity (71% religious vs 59% not)

our_assessment.why: Reproduces exactly. Narrower in what the number IS: a lifetime-ever item that does not behave like a lifetime cumulative risk. It is 21% already among those practising under a year and 28% after twenty years. A constant hazard predicts roughly 2% rising to 62%; adding quitting after an event (k = 0.09/yr) or recall decay (10%/yr) still predicts a rising curve from about 2-3%. Only a front-loaded, early-onset subgroup (about a quarter, experiencing it within the first months) reproduces the flat shape (reanalysis/m4.py). So the 25.6% describes who is prone, early, among people who kept practising -- it cannot be projected as 'risk accumulated over a meditative career', and it says nothing about people who stopped, whom the design excludes and the paper never mentions. Completion before the item was 65% and differed by continent and religiosity.

claims.statement: Meditators who engaged only in deconstructive practices (e.g. vipassana/insight) had 65% higher odds of unpleasant experiences than those who engaged only in attentional and/or constructive practices (OR 1.65, 95% CI 1.12-2.42), and retreat experience was associated with higher odds (OR 1.68, 1.27-2.23).
claims.scope: Univariable logistic regressions; the meditation-type contrast excludes the 499 (40.5%) who practise both deconstructive and non-deconstructive types.

quantities.name: meditation_unpleasant_experience_prevalence_mixed_types
quantities.baseline: deconstructive AND attentional/constructive -- the group the paper excluded; OR 1.69 vs non-deconstructive, p = 0.0003

quantities.name: deconstructive_only_odds_ratio_adjusted_for_retreat
quantities.baseline: deconstructive-only vs non-deconstructive, adjusted for retreat; + sex, religiosity, PTQ, age, years: 1.33 (0.86-2.06), p = 0.20. 80.7% of the deconstructive-only group had retreat experience vs 45.1% of the non-deconstructive group

quantities.name: retreat_odds_ratio_adjusted_for_years_band
quantities.baseline: retreat ever vs never, adjusted for six bands of years of practice; in the full multivariable model with meditation type 1.73 (1.16-2.58)

our_assessment.why: The retreat association is the robust one: it survives adjustment for years of practice (retreat attendance rises from 33% to 92% across year bands while the outcome does not move), for meditation type and for the demographic predictors, and it is visible even in the first year (27% with a retreat vs 18% without). The 'deconstructive' association is not separable from it: adjusted for retreat it falls to 1.41 (p = 0.10). And the exclusion the paper justifies as conceptual hides a dose-response test that fails: the excluded mixed group has the SAME prevalence as the deconstructive-only group (30.1% vs 29.5%). If deconstructive practice drove the experiences, doing only that should not look identical to doing it alongside other practices. Cross-sectional, so 'retreat' may still be a marker (seriousness, teacher contact, intention) rather than a cause, as the authors themselves note.

claims.statement: Higher repetitive negative thinking was associated with unpleasant experiences, 'although the estimate for this association was small in magnitude' (Table 2: OR 1.02 per '1 SD', 1.00-1.03).
claims.scope: Univariable logistic regression on the PTQ total (range 0-60, sample SD 9.49).

quantities.name: repetitive_negative_thinking_odds_ratio_per_sd
quantities.unit: odds ratio per SD of PTQ (9.49 points)
quantities.baseline: same model as Table 2 rescaled; the printed 1.02 is per ONE PTQ POINT (Stata `logistic negative ptq`), mislabelled '1 SD'

quantities.name: repetitive_negative_thinking_odds_ratio_per_point
quantities.baseline: as fitted by the authors' code

our_assessment.why: The association is real and the code is right; the table header is wrong and the prose built on it is wrong. Table 2 labels PTQ, mindfulness and self-compassion '(1 SD)' while its own footnote and the .do file use one raw unit. For PTQ that turns OR 1.16 per SD -- about the size of the sex difference read the other way (1/0.75 = 1.33) -- into a printed 1.02 that the Discussion then calls 'small in magnitude'. For mindfulness and self-compassion the mislabel runs the other way and is harmless (per SD 1.01 and 0.96, both null). A unit error that changes the paper's own verbal verdict on a predictor.

claims.statement: No association between unpleasant experiences and lifetime meditation experience (OR 1.00 per year, p = 0.74), frequency or session length.
claims.scope: Univariable logistic regressions, years of regular practice as a linear term.

quantities.name: lifetime_practice_years_odds_ratio_per_sd
quantities.baseline: as fitted; log(years): OR 1.055 per e-fold, p = 0.29

our_assessment.why: Reported as an absence of association, discussed against two studies that found practice-amount effects. It is better read as a strong STRUCTURAL result about the outcome item. For a 'have you ever' question, exposure time should raise prevalence mechanically unless something removes or prevents later cases; that it does not is the most informative pattern in the data (see c1 and the known-answer stories in reanalysis/m4.py). The null is about what the item measures and who remains in the sample, not about whether practice amount is harmless.

artifacts.locator: https://osf.io/d6mgj/ (child component 'Data' of osf.io/gj7z2): UnpleasantMeditation_Raw data.xlsx (2,599 starters, 79 cols) and UnpleasantMeditation_Clean data.xlsx (1,281 rows; 1,232 after the script's two drop rules)

checked.result: 2/2 sha256+md5 verified. Clean file + the .do's two drop rules give N = 1,232 and 315 events exactly. The RAW file lets the dropout funnel be measured (2,599 -> 1,688 reached the outcome item), which the paper reports only as counts.

datasheet.composition: One row per respondent; demographics, practice variables, item-level PTQ/SCS/Mindsens, binary outcome 'negative'. Codebook sheet in the clean file.
datasheet.collection: Opinio online survey, April-August 2017, no payment.
datasheet.caveats: The parent OSF node is EMPTY; the data live in child components (a reader following the DAS link sees no files). No licence declared. Years of practice is self-reported with 0.16-year resolution for the 2-month floor.

checked.how: read; ported line by line to reanalysis/m1.py
checked.result: Every Table 2 estimate reproduces. Confirms the continuous predictors are fitted per raw unit (`logistic negative ptq`), contradicting the '(1 SD)' labels in Table 2.

relations.why: Both treat 'meditation type' as a category a practitioner belongs to. Here 48% of practitioners use more than one family and the 40% who mix deconstructive with other types are excluded as 'conceptually too broad' -- yet they carry exactly the deconstructive-only prevalence. A practitioner-level type variable is mostly a proxy for depth of engagement (retreats), which is what the CAT project's dimensional scoring of practices, rather than practitioners, is meant to avoid.

open_questions: Is the flat lifetime-prevalence curve replicated in the other two surveys the paper cites (Cebolla et al. 2017, n = 342, 25.4%; Vieten et al. 2018, n = 1,120, 32%)? If their data are open, the same years-band table decides between 'early-onset susceptibility' and sampling artifacts specific to this survey.

A survey that includes people who STOPPED meditating would measure what this design cannot: whether unpleasant experiences predict discontinuation. That is the denominator every prevalence figure in this literature is missing.
Outcome item asked after 60 rumination / self-compassion / mindfulness items: is there a priming effect on reporting? Testable only by a design that randomises item order.
